transcript.text: Indesit washer dryer washes fine but the drying cycle doesn't get warm at all, clothes come out cold and wet after 2 hours. Model is XWDE 96 something.

It sounds like the heater isn't engaging, which is often due to restricted airflow tripping a safety cut-out or simply the dryer being overloaded. Please make sure you are drying no more than half the load size used for washing, as putting a full wash load straight into dry will leave clothes damp. Also check that a proper drying programme was selected and not just a short timed dry. First, please switch off and unplug the machine before checking the lint filter at the bottom front; if it is blocked with fluff, clean it thoroughly. Second, ensure the cold water tap behind the machine is fully on, as these units need a trickle of cold water to condense moisture during drying. Let me know what you find with those two checks.

I can hear water trickling at the back during the dry, so the water seems fine. The load is about 4kg and I had it on standard cotton dry, timed 120 min. I'm not sure what the lint filter looks like on this one, where exactly is it? No burning smell and nothing tripping, by the way.

The lint filter on your Indesit XWDE 96 SOMETHING is located at the bottom of the door opening, usually hidden behind a small plastic flap or grille. Please switch off and unplug the machine before removing it to clean away any fluff buildup that might be blocking airflow. Since the water supply is working, a clogged filter could be causing the dryer to overheat and cut out the heat as a safety measure. Once you have cleaned the filter, run a short test cycle and let me know if the air coming from the drum feels warm.

Ok, I'll unplug it and look for the filter. Also the door glass and drum stay stone cold during the dry, and I should say I unplugged it mid-cycle last week to grab a shirt, and it stopped heating after that.

The fact that it stopped heating after you unplugged it mid-cycle suggests the thermal cut-out may have tripped and needs time to reset, or there is a deeper fault. Please check the condenser unit behind the bottom flap at the front of the machine; this is often clogged with fluff on these models. Unplug the dryer, remove the condenser, rinse it under the tap until clean, and let it dry completely before refitting it securely. This will ensure proper airflow and help rule out an overheating safety cut-out.
[Helpful to see: image "Where the condenser and water tank are" — On a condenser dryer the water container pulls out at the top and the condenser/heat exchanger sits behind a flap at the bottom front — slide it out and rinse it. Condenser/heat-pump dryers only; layout may differ.]
Ok, I can try the condenser. Is there something else I should be looking at though, since the drum is stone cold and the fan is running? I'm happy to take the top panel off if that helps.

It could be the heater element has failed open, which would explain why the drum stays stone cold even though the fan is running. Since you are comfortable removing panels, the next step is to check for continuity on the heating element and its thermal cut-out using a multimeter. First, switch off and unplug the machine, then remove the top panel by taking out the two screws at the back. You will find the heater assembly near the drum; disconnect it and test the resistance across the terminals of both the heater element and the thermal cut-out. If either shows no continuity (infinite resistance), that part is faulty and needs replacing.

I don't have a multimeter so I can't test continuity. I can unplug it and take the top off to look though. I can see a heater box with wires and a small round button-like part on top, but I can't tell if it's blown. Is there anything else I can check without a meter?

Without a multimeter, you can't test for electrical faults like a broken heater element or thermal cut-out, so we have to focus on airflow and sensor issues. The small round button-like part you see is likely the thermal cut-out, which cannot be visually inspected for being "blown" without testing it electrically. Since you have already checked the water supply and cleaned the condenser, the next best check is to ensure the moisture sensors inside the drum are clean. These are usually two metal strips near where the lint filter sits; if they are coated with fabric conditioner residue, the dryer may not sense when clothes are dry and stop heating prematurely. Wipe them gently with a damp cloth and some white vinegar to remove any buildup. If cleaning these doesn't help, it is likely that the heater element has failed internally and will need replacement by an engineer.
Ok, I'll wipe the metal strips with the damp cloth and vinegar. If that doesn't work, should I get an engineer in for the heater, or is there something else to try first?

If cleaning the sensors doesn't restore heat, you will need an engineer because the heater element or thermal cut-out is likely failed and requires replacement. Since you cannot test these parts without a multimeter, it is safest to get a professional to diagnose and fix the electrical fault. You can arrange this by calling Indesit support or using a local appliance repair service in your area. Before they come, please ensure the condenser is clean and the lint filter is clear so they have the best chance of identifying the issue quickly.
